messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Construction Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Darnell, a 39-year-old divorced construction worker, came to treatment after months of feeling as if the ground beneath his life had become untrustworthy. The event that marked the beginning was not something that happened to him directly, but something he witnessed on a jobsite. One afternoon, while working on a commercial build, he saw a coworker fall from a scaffold and hit the lower levels hard enough that the scene was instantly chaotic and irreversible. Darnell described the memory less as a story than as a sequence of pictures that still arrived without warning: the angle of the fall, the body on the concrete, the way everyone froze for a second before rushing in. What stayed with him most was not just what he saw but the sensory sharpness of it. When the images came back, he could smell the dusty, metallic odor that had hung in the air and taste the bitter residue that was in his mouth that day, as though his body had kept the event more faithfully than his words ever could.

From the start, Darnell made sense of the trauma through a bleak conviction that the world no longer worked by any rules he could trust. He said his beliefs about how things are supposed to go had been “completely destroyed,” because a routine workday had turned into an emergency before he could do anything to stop it. He was certain that bad things could happen anywhere, at any time, and that there was nothing he could do to prevent them. That sense of helplessness bled into how he saw himself as well; he felt inadequate for not reacting fast enough, not doing enough, not being the kind of man who could keep people safe. Those appraisals made the vivid recollections feel even more charged. When the images returned, they seemed to confirm his fears: if he could still see it so clearly, if he could still smell and taste that day, then the event had not really passed and the danger it revealed was still present.

As the weeks went on, Darnell tried to keep those feelings from surfacing at all. He said he never allowed himself to feel or express anger, even when he was irritable or resentful, because anger seemed dangerous and pointless in a world that had already shown him how little control he had. He also began gambling after work, using the rush of risk and excitement to pull his attention away from what he had seen and from the shame he carried about it. At times he would deliberately try to leave his body or blank out, sitting in his truck after shifts and forcing himself to go numb for a few minutes before going home. These habits were not random to him; they were ways of getting away from the images and the beliefs that came with them. If he let himself think about the fall, he said, he would be right back inside that helpless moment, feeling again that his own inadequacy had made him powerless.

In his day-to-day life, Darnell’s job kept placing him near the same kinds of cues that set things off. Scaffolds, hard hats, the smell of concrete dust, even the sharp taste of coffee gone cold in the middle of a long shift could bring back the scene in fragments. When that happened, he would work harder at pushing everything down, tightening his jaw, staying silent, and later looking for a way to escape the feeling by gambling or shutting himself off mentally. The more the memory intruded, the more proof he felt he had that the world could break open without warning and that he was not equipped to stop it. That, in turn, made him withdraw further into these habits, because he had come to believe that if he stayed emotionally flat and distracted, he might avoid being overwhelmed by how little control he actually had. Over time, this left him feeling cut off from coworkers and distant from his ex-wife and teenage son, who noticed that he had become harder to reach and quicker to disappear into himself.

By the time he sought help, Darnell was exhausted by the cycle of images, dread, and escape. He said he was tired of living as if he were always waiting for the next collapse, and he was frightened that his son was beginning to see him as absent and inadequate in the same way he had come to see himself. What brought him in was the sense that the gambling, the blanking out, and the constant suppression were no longer giving him relief, only shrinking his life. He hoped treatment might help him feel less trapped by the pictures that kept returning, and he was most afraid that if he could not change, he would remain stuck believing that nothing and no one could be trusted, including himself.
